problems.form_value: individual (the same block's what_was_assigned adds: 'The paper does not say how the ideation factor was assigned within sessions, or whether the two members of a pair could be in different ideation conditions.')
problems.source_says: Not established for 137 of the 212 analyzed people. The only basis for 'individual' is the p. 4 sentence that participants were randomly assigned to one of the four conditions. Page 5 shows that sentence does not hold for the teammate factor, which was set per session: two people who came to the same session were paired and both anticipated a human teammate, and a person who came alone anticipated an AI teammate. For the ideation factor the paper names no allocation rule, and neither the text nor Fig. 1 says whether the two members of a pair could get different ideation conditions. So in the human-teammate cells (69 + 68) the unit that received Co-pilot may be the person or the session pair. Criterion 1 holds either way, but the codebook's standard-error rule (clusters when assignment is clustered) depends on it. Suggested coding: 'other', noting 'individual for people who came alone; for pairs the paper does not say whether the ideation condition was set per person or per session'.
problems.quote: When two participants arrived for the same session, they were paired with each other, and the presence of one another human served as a cue for their future teammate.
problems.locator: p. 5, Section 4.2 (Study design); p. 4, Section 4 (Method); p. 9, Fig. 1; text-layer search of pp. 1-10 for random*, assign*, allocat*, counterbalanc*, stratif*

problems.form_value: 'participants who arrived together for a session were paired and anticipated each other'; the summary says the teammate factor 'was set by whether a participant arrived alone or with another participant'
problems.source_says: Minor wording. The paper says two participants 'arrived for the same session', that pairing followed the sign-up schedule, and that paired participants were strangers. 'Arrived together' and 'arrived ... with another participant' can be read as coming as a pair of acquaintances, which the paper rules out. Suggested wording: 'participants who signed up for and attended the same session were paired'. No coded value changes.
problems.quote: Participants who anticipated a human teammate were paired randomly according to the sign-up schedule. ... Paired participants were strangers and did not know each other prior to the study.

problems.form_value: Participants used Co-pilot as an assisting tool, asking 'what' and 'how' questions to get ideas or suggestions. They had to type out their own ideas in a Word document and could not use AI-generated responses verbatim (pp. 4-5, Sections 4.2-4.3).
problems.source_says: Minor. The paper gives the 'what' and 'how' questions and the no-verbatim rule as instructions. It reports no measure of how participants used Co-pilot or whether they followed the rule, and it says the chat histories were deleted after data collection. The Word document is named only in Section 4.4 (p. 5), outside the cited Sections 4.2-4.3. Suggested wording: 'Participants were instructed to use Co-pilot as an assisting tool ... (p. 5, Sections 4.2-4.4). No usage or compliance measure is reported.' Criterion 1 is not affected.
problems.quote: Participants in the AI-assisted condition were instructed to use Microsoft Co-Pilot as an assisting tool by asking “what” and “how” questions to generate ideas.
problems.locator: p. 5, Section 4.3 (Procedure); p. 5, Section 4.2 (standardized instructions); p. 5, Section 4.4 (Word document)

confirmed.statement: The document states random assignment once: participants 'were randomly assigned to one of the four conditions' of the 2 × 2. A text-layer search of all 10 pages finds no other such statement. The other uses of 'random' concern pairing by sign-up schedule and the distribution of ideas and participants among coders. The abstract says only 'In a laboratory experiment (N = 212)'.
confirmed.locator: p. 4, Section 4 (Method); p. 5, Sections 4.2 and 4.4; p. 1, Abstract

confirmed.statement: The form's randomized = yes follows the document (form-spec rule 1), and the form already records each weakness of that sentence. The teammate factor was set by attendance. The counts 69/68/37/38 attached to the sentence are post-exclusion counts (they sum to the 212 analyzed, while 224 were recruited and 12 were excluded after taking part). No allocation rule is given for the ideation factor. The paper also does not say how conditions were spread across the two semesters of data collection or the 'larger project', which the form's open question on the mechanism covers.
confirmed.locator: p. 4, Sections 4 and 4.1; p. 5, Sections 4.2 and 4.4

confirmed.statement: What was assigned is access to a generative-AI tool for the participant's own work. In the AI-assisted condition participants used Microsoft Co-pilot (Auto mode) during the 10-minute individual brainstorming, and every scored outcome comes from the ideas each participant typed. The conditions do not differ only in whose output is evaluated.

The tool is generative AI. The paper calls Co-pilot 'a university-licensed generative AI system', participants queried it as a chat assistant through individual accounts, and the paper describes GenAI as built on large language models. No underlying model is named in the 10 pages, as name_model says.
confirmed.locator: p. 4, Section 4.2; p. 5, Sections 4.2-4.3; p. 1, Introduction; text-layer search of pp. 1-10

confirmed.statement: The comparison arms match the form. 'In the independent ideation condition, participants brainstormed alone', after the same IDEO video and printed brainstorming rules as the AI arms, so ai = none and ai_vs_bau fit. In HAT and AI-HAT the AI teammate is only anticipated for a later session, and the scored ideas in HAT were produced without AI.
The paper calls the design a '2 × 2 between-subjects design', so check (e) on the order of conditions does not apply and structure = between is right.

The arrival-based teammate factor does not confound the AI contrasts. Within each teammate group the AI split is 68 vs 69 and 38 vs 37, so each simple-effect contrast compares arms of the same arrival type. The pooled contrast has nearly the same mix in both arms (68 and 69 of 106 with a human teammate). The form lists no teammate contrasts, which is right.
Arm names, descriptions, and n_analyzed (69, 68, 37, 38) match the paper's labels and counts. n_randomized = null is right, because the paper gives no count at assignment.
confirmed.locator: p. 4, Section 4 and Hypothesis 3a; p. 9, Fig. 1

confirmed.statement: The form's assignment quote is verbatim and its locators are right (random-assignment sentence on p. 4, Section 4; teammate set by arrival on p. 5, Section 4.2). preregistered = yes is right: Data availability on p. 9, Hypotheses 1 (p. 3) and 2 (p. 4) labeled pre-registered, Hypotheses 3a and 3b labeled non-preregistered (p. 4).
Fig. 1 is a conceptual diagram of the four conditions. It shows no allocation step, and its AI-HHT icon (one monitor between two people) does not show whether both members of a pair had Co-pilot.

summary: The PDF states once that participants were randomly assigned to the cells of a 2 × 2 between-subjects design whose first factor is brainstorming alone versus with Microsoft Co-pilot, a generative-AI chat system, on each participant's own scored ideas (p. 4), and nothing in the text shows the AI factor was allocated non-randomly, so criterion 1 holds, although it rests on a sentence that the paper itself shows is wrong for the arrival-based teammate factor (p. 5). The coding is refuted only in detail: unit = individual is not established for the 137 paired participants, because the paper never says whether the two members of a session pair could get different ideation conditions, and two free-text fields have minor wording or locator slips.
